title.narrative: Developing a sustainable and fair coffee supply chain in Nariño, Colombia

description.narrative: Nariño is one of the poorest areas of Colombia. Post-conflict, over 43.6% of people in the area still suffer extreme poverty and coffee production is one of the key industries in the region. Kinti Café is a social entrepreneurial coffee company offering the best available specialty coffee that is sourced directly from our smallholder farms and with that immediately contributes to the positive and peaceful transformation of Colombia. Locally, Kinti Café works with social coffee federation Asprounión that represents 200 local coffee farmers. Together they considerably improve the livelihood of farmers involved through their unique model: direct trade and fair chain in which the coffee farmers themselves co-benefit from the profits generated through the international sales of roasted coffees, as oppose to solely the sales of their beans. By adding value to the coffee, the consortium also aims to inspire youth and post conflict communities to find a future in sustainable coffee farming. Due to the increasing demand for ‘fair’ trade and single origin specialty coffees, to enable impact from the start onwards and to prepare for future investments, Technical Assistance (DGGF-TA) is currently providing support to Kinti and Asprounión in order to generate profitable and inclusive business with a positive impact on the entire coffee supply chain (fair supply chain development). The project includes improving processes and quality of sustainable organic coffee farming and local roasting, creating access to the European market by pre-financing and shipment of the first containers of green beans and conducting market research and developing a sustainable, inclusive and circular supply chain. The project directly supports 42 jobs, of which almost half is woman and almost all involves youth. Indirectly the project supports 200 small holder coffee farmers. Knowledge transfer is an important part of the project and is done training these coffee farmers about different aspects of adding value to the coffee they produce. Furthermore, 60 small holder coffee farmers receive training to switch from traditional coffee farming to organic coffee farming and how to comply with international standards in order to prepare for certification in 2020. The number of jobs and farmers supported is expected to rise during the project. Upon successful completion further investments are planned as well as replication of the model to other DGGF countries.
